structure.title: Introduction and chapters 1–6 · From the first stars to the first critics
structure.text: Khemani and Chipkin begin by counting the immense stretches of time during which stars made more stars. They then turn the same question on human history. How could a society keep its customs intact for generations, even when changing one of them might have saved lives? The opening chapters make continuity itself something to explain.

structure.title: Chapter 7: The Big Bang – Multicellularity · Life learns to keep a discovery
structure.text: The history starts over at the scale of a molecule. A replicator can pass something on, a cell can incorporate another living system, and cooperating cells can make a creature whose parts do different jobs. Each episode asks what a new arrangement made physically possible for its descendants.

structure.title: Chapter 7: Universal Explainers – The Universal Computer · Money, elections and engines enter the same history
structure.text: Once people can explain how things work, a useful discovery can travel between strangers and survive the discoverer. Money allows exchanges that would otherwise fail. Elections allow rulers to be replaced. Putting these beside engines and computers lets the authors make a claim about institutions as human inventions with consequences as tangible as machines.

structure.title: Chapters 8–9 · The timeline runs past the present
structure.text: The headings continue on into immortality, artificial general intelligence and proposed political arrangements. The typography makes them look like neighbours of the steam engine. Their standing changes nevertheless. A reader now has to assess an argument that something could be achieved, and sometimes a further argument that it ought to be.

people.name: Static and dynamic societies
people.role: Two ways of transmitting an inheritance
people.text: Both kinds of society teach children things their ancestors knew. In the authors' distinction, what matters is whether the customs being passed on also let a child question them. A society can possess remarkable skills and still make it exceedingly difficult to correct an inherited mistake.

people.name: David Deutsch
people.role: Physicist whose account of knowledge informs the book
people.text: For Deutsch, knowing how to do something changes which physical transformations people can bring about. The authors extend this idea across a history in which the same planet successively supports bacteria, engines and computers. Their more specific social proposals are claims they must make in their own right.

context.title: What optimism commits the authors to
context.text: Calling a problem soluble leaves a great deal open. People can die before the solution is found, and suppressing criticism can keep it out of reach. The authors' optimism puts the burden on anyone who says a difficulty is permanent to explain what makes it so.

context.title: How a custom protects itself
context.text: A practice can survive because it works well. It can also survive because people who question it are punished or never get to teach the next generation. The authors use this second possibility to explain how customs that cause suffering can remain astonishingly durable even among people with strong reasons to change them.

passages.quote: For humans, suffering is intimately related to staticity.

notice.text: Follow the passage from copying to correcting.
notice.why: A gene, a custom and a scientific explanation can all outlive the individual that carries them. Only some of the book's examples involve someone deliberately trying to find a mistake. That difference bears much of the weight of its account of progress.

notice.text: Ask what is being counted during the opening billions of years.
notice.why: The authors call an age monotonous because familiar kinds of astronomical objects keep recurring. A star can change enormously during that interval. Their story depends on a particular measure of novelty, and they carry that choice of measure forward into the history of civilisation.

opening: A planet can contain everything needed for a civilisation without producing one. Materials wait; knowledge changes what can be done with them. Arjun Khemani and Logan Chipkin use that distinction to argue for a future far larger than current resources and technologies suggest. Their optimism rests on the creation of explanations and the institutions that allow criticism to improve them. The provocation is that humanity's greatest limitations may lie in ideas that can be replaced, while treating those limitations as permanent helps preserve them.
